title: Coming in 2027: Apple’s $1,000 home robot for FaceTime and switching on lights
gist: Per The Information, Apple CEO John Ternus is backing a roaming AI home robot code-named J595 (possibly HomeView Ultra) aimed at a 2027 launch at $1,000 or more, with possible delays to 2028. The author is skeptical about demand, noting thin features and a robotics team of only about 10 true roboticists next to roughly 300 software staff.

insights.claim: Apple's new CEO John Ternus is reportedly pushing household robots, and the first may be a roaming robot that supports FaceTime calls and turns lights on when a person enters a room.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Robotics would be a new hardware category for Apple under its new CEO and a possible signal of long-term capital allocation.

insights.claim: The AI-driven robot, code-named J595, could be named HomeView Ultra to match Apple's stationary HomeView smart display, and Apple reportedly aims to launch it by 2027 at $1,000 or more, though delays could push it to 2028.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: The timeline and price set the earliest point at which robotics could contribute revenue and suggest a premium-only market position.

insights.claim: The earliest prototypes appeared in 2018 and former CEO Tim Cook approved continuing the project. Engineers have spent years trying to give it more than a 'fancy way to make FaceTime calls' so it can justify a high price.

insights.so_what: A program running for eight years without a clear use case points to product-market-fit risk.

insights.claim: Ternus is also backing a separate Apple project for robots that do household tasks such as folding clothes, which would presumably need arms and manipulators. It is unclear whether Apple wants a general-purpose humanoid like those from 1X and Figure AI.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A possible Apple entry into household manipulation robots could become competition for humanoid startups such as 1X and Figure AI.

insights.claim: The author argues the robot's reported features look underwhelming next to existing smart home devices, or even a robot vacuum with a clearer household use case, and questions whether there is a market for a $1,000-plus mobile FaceTime device.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: This is a demand risk for a premium home robot and a caution against assuming Apple's brand alone creates a new category.

insights.claim: The author holds that a limited-purpose home robot makes much more sense technically and for safety than a general-purpose autonomous robot near humans, but the open question is whether enough customers will pay Apple's price.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Narrow-scope robots lower execution risk, but pricing power is unproven, which frames how to value consumer robotics.
insights.quote: The question is whether Apple can find enough customers willing to pay whatever it charges for a limited-purpose home robot.

insights.so_what: Thin hardware robotics talent suggests Apple may rely on acquisitions or hiring to compete in robotics, and it raises execution risk.
